title: City of God (2002 film)
description: 2002 Brazilian epic crime film by Fernando Meirelles and Kátia Lund
wiki_lead:
City of God (Portuguese: Cidade de Deus) is a 2002 Brazilian epic crime film directed by Fernando Meirelles and co-directed by Kátia Lund. The screenplay, written by Bráulio Mantovani, is adapted from the 1997 novel of the same name by Paulo Lins, though the plot is also loosely based on real events. The film portrays the rise of organized crime in the Cidade de Deus suburb of Rio de Janeiro between the late 1960s and early 1980s, culminating in a war between drug dealer Li'l Zé and vigilante-turned-criminal Knockout Ned. Its tagline is, "If you run, the beast catches you; if you stay, the beast eats you."
The film features a cast including Alexandre Rodrigues, Leandro Firmino, Jonathan and Phellipe Haagensen, Douglas Silva, Daniel Zettel, Seu Jorge, and the film debut of Alice Braga. Most of the actors were actual residents of favelas such as Vidigal and Cidade de Deus itself.
City of God received widespread critical acclaim and earned four nominations at the 76th Academy Awards: Best Cinematography (César Charlone), Best Director (Meirelles), Best Film Editing (Daniel Rezende), and Best Adapted Screenplay (Mantovani). At the previous 75th Academy Awards, it was Brazil's submission for the Academy Award for Best International Feature Film but was not selected as a finalist. In 2015, the Brazilian Film Critics Association (Abraccine) ranked City of God 8th on its list of the 100 greatest Brazilian films.
Following the success of City of God, Meirelles and Lund created the City of Men TV series and its 2007 film adaptation. Both projects share some actors (notably leads Silva and Darlan Cunha) and the same setting as City of God.

Plot
An armed gang chases after an escaped chicken in a favela called the City of God. The chicken stops between the gang and a young man nicknamed Rocket.
In the 1960s, three impoverished, amateur thieves known as the "Tender Trio"—Shaggy, Clipper, and Rocket's older brother, Goose—rob business owners and share the money with the community who, in turn, hide them from the police.
Li'l Dice, a young boy, convinces them to hold up a motel and rob its occupants. The gang resolves not to kill anyone and tells Li'l Dice to be a lookout. Instead, Li'l Dice guns down the motel occupants after falsely warning the trio that the police are coming. The massacre attracts so much police attention that the trio is forced to split up: Clipper joins the Church, Shaggy is shot by the police while trying to escape the favela, and Goose is shot by Li'l Dice after taking his money while Li'l Dice's friend Benny, Shaggy's brother, watches.
In the 1970s, Rocket has joined a group of young hippies. He enjoys photography and likes one girl, Angélica, but his attempt to get close to her is ruined by a gang of petty criminal kids known as "The Runts". grok_lead: City of God (Portuguese: Cidade de Deus) is a 2002 Brazilian crime drama film co-directed by Fernando Meirelles and KÃ¡tia Lund, with a screenplay by BrÃ¡ulio Mantovani adapted from the 1997 semi-autobiographical novel of the same name by Paulo Lins, who drew from his experiences growing up in the favela. The narrative spans three decades in Rio de Janeiro's Cidade de Deus housing project, chronicling the transformation of petty theft among youth in the 1960s into entrenched drug trafficking and inter-gang warfare by the 1980s, centered on characters like aspiring photographer Rocket and his encounters with figures such as the psychopathic Li'l ZÃ©. Filmed primarily in adjacent favelas due to the site's persistent dangers, the production employed numerous non-professional actors recruited from Rio's slums, lending a raw authenticity to depictions of daily violence, poverty, and survival strategies amid absent state authority. The film's kinetic editing, vibrant cinematography by CÃ©sar Charlone, and nonlinear structure emulate the chaotic rhythm of favela life, drawing stylistic influences from sources like Goodfellas while grounding events in empirical observations of crime's socioeconomic roots. Upon release, City of God garnered international acclaim for its unflinching realism, earning a 91% approval rating from critics and four Academy Award nominations, including Best Director for Meirelles, Best Cinematography, Best Film Editing, and Best Adapted Screenplay. In Brazil, it won multiple honors at festivals like the SESC Film Festival, though some local voices, including rapper MV Bill from the favela itself, criticized it for potentially reinforcing external stereotypes of slum dwellers as inherently violent, thereby overshadowing structural causes like political neglect. Despite such debates, the film catalyzed global awareness of favela dynamics, influencing subsequent works and underscoring how unchecked criminal economies flourish in governance vacuums.
